title: The bardo
hook: teachings on the in-between after death; a text read aloud to the dying

segments.voice: Yesterday: exile, a tradition carried over the mountains, a sorrow held with care. Your line: carried into exile.

A favorite song. A psalm. A letter from a grandchild. In hospice rooms, near the end, families sometimes read or play something to the one who is dying. Hospice staff are taught that hearing may be among the last senses to fade. Tibetan Buddhists have a whole text for that moment, read aloud beside the dying, and then beside the body for days afterward. It speaks directly to the one who has died, in a calm voice, telling them where they are.
screen: `A SONG, A PSALM, A LETTER.` → `HEARING, AMONG THE LAST TO FADE.` → `A TEXT READ ALOUD BESIDE THE DYING.`

segments.voice: Bardo is Tibetan for the in-between, a gap between one state and the next. Tibetan teachers describe several: the in-between of this life, of dreams, of meditation, of dying, and then, after death, the stages before a new birth. They teach that this last passage can last up to forty-nine days. First, they say, comes a moment of clear light, like a cloudless sky. If it isn't recognized, visions arise, peaceful and then fierce, and finally the mind is drawn toward a new life. The text that guides this is called, in Tibetan, Liberation Through Hearing in the In-Between. Tradition says Padmasambhava composed it and hid it, and that a treasure-finder named Karma Lingpa found it centuries later. In the West it's known as The Tibetan Book of the Dead, a title given by its first English editor. A lama or friend reads it near the one who has died, and its message, over and over, is simple: don't be afraid; these appearances are your own mind; recognize them, and be free. Buddhist traditions differ here. The Theravada Abhidhamma teaches that rebirth follows immediately, without an in-between, though some Theravada teachers allow for one. The Tibetan schools, and some other Mahayana traditions, teach the in-between in detail, and East Asian Buddhist rites also mark forty-nine days after a death. And Tibetan teachers add one more thing: every moment is a kind of bardo. Between jobs, between homes, between one breath and the next, things loosen, and change becomes possible. In between.
screen: `BARDO — THE IN-BETWEEN.` · `CLEAR LIGHT, THEN VISIONS.` · `LIBERATION THROUGH HEARING.` · `EVERY MOMENT A KIND OF BARDO.` · then, large: `IN BETWEEN.`

segments.voice: This one asks for a gentle heart, so go easy: if you're willing, let one thing come that you'd want read to you at the very end, a verse, a song, a few words from someone you love, without deciding anything. Then let it go, and rest in the small gap at the end of each out-breath, the tiny in-between before the next breath comes.
Bardo. The in-between: in Tibetan teaching, the passage between death and rebirth, and every gap where change becomes possible.
Your line: in between. Every moment, Tibetan teachers say, is a kind of bardo. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Tibetan communities a lama or trained friend often reads the Bardo Thödol aloud beside the dying and, after death, beside the body, and families hold rituals during the forty-nine days that follow; many Theravada communities hold merit-making ceremonies for the dead instead.

original.note: Tibetan bar do: the in-between, the gap between one state and the next.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Tibetan word for the afterlife.
what it means: an in-between: after death, and also every gap in life where change can happen.

what a scholar hears: bar do is often glossed 'between two'; the Bardo Thödol is a 'treasure' (terma) text, and Evans-Wentz named it The Tibetan Book of the Dead in 1927 after the Egyptian Book of the Dead.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer opens on an unsourced generalization ('Hospice nurses will tell you... people often ask'); now opens on the objects and hedges the hearing claim; cut 'fourteenth century' and '1927' from the voice and myth; Theravada view attributed to the Abhidhamma (Kathavatthu rejects an intermediate state) with a note that some Theravada teachers allow one, replacing 'many Theravada teachers'; East Asian forty-nine-day rites stated without 'families'.
The Evans-Wentz / Kazi Dawa Samdup 1927 English version may be public domain in the US, but its exact wording isn't quoted here.
The number and names of the bardos vary (four or six in different teachings): kept general.
Theravada view of immediate rebirth: some Theravada teachers allow an intermediate period; framed as 'many Theravada teachers'. Confirm.
'Hearing may be one of the last senses to fade' is a common hospice observation; kept hedged with 'may'.
Sensitive topic: practice is phrased gently and optionally.
